content: The evaluation process involves collaboration among government representatives, development partners, academia, and civil society. According to the United Nations Evaluation Group (UNEG), evaluation is defined as a systematic and impartial assessment of an activity, project, program, strategy, policy, theme, sector, operational area, or institutional performance. It examines both expected and achieved outcomes by analyzing the results chain, processes, contextual factors, and causal links to understand successes or shortcomings. The purpose is to assess the relevance, impact, effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability of interventions and contributions made by UN system organizations. The Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) evaluation aims to assess the World Health Organization’s (WHO) contributions to and influence on national health development agendas, as aligned with the agreed joint strategic priorities outlined in the CCS. This evaluation is a structured, decentralized process conducted across all levels of the organization. Its primary objective is to evaluate the effectiveness, efficiency, and quality of WHO’s work in improving health outcomes in a specific country. Additionally, it informs the development of new CCS strategies. While part of WHO’s broader accountability framework, CCS evaluation is distinct from other supervisory functions, such as audits, as it focuses on results, understanding what works, and documenting the reasons and mechanisms behind successes or failures. Unlike program budget monitoring, CCS evaluation also considers relevance, context, causality, impact, and sustainability. The CCS evaluation adheres to WHO’s five key evaluation principles: impartiality, independence, utility, quality, and transparency. It also incorporates overarching principles such as a human rights-based approach, gender mainstreaming, and equity in health. The general objective of the evaluation is to substantiate WHO’s contributions to achieving results and to generate recommendations that influence policy, management, and operational decisions at the country level. The evaluation has five specific objectives: 1. Review the progress, processes, outputs, and outcomes of CCS priorities. 2. Examine the alignment of CCS priorities with the government’s health agenda. 3. Determine the impact of WHO’s work under the current CCS on the country’s health outcomes. 4. Analyze the harmonization of WHO’s work with other UN agencies through the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF). 5. Identify lessons learned from planning and implementing the current CCS to inform the development of the next CCS. The evaluation results should provide insights into the effectiveness, relevance, efficiency, impact, and sustainability of CCS interventions. Evaluation questions should assess the logic of the CCS theory of change and determine whether its result framework is credible. These questions should address progress made, WHO’s contributions, alignment with government priorities, and the impact on health outcomes. They should also explore challenges, lessons learned, and missed opportunities, as well as the adequacy of resources mobilized for implementation. The evaluation methodology involves a hybrid approach, including desk reviews of relevant documents, stakeholder interviews, and participatory methods. Data collection and analysis occur in three phases: 1. A desk review of national and partner documents to assess intervention logic and contextual factors. 2. Qualitative data collection through interviews and focus group discussions with key stakeholders. 3. Feedback sessions with senior national health authorities and other stakeholders. The evaluation process is participatory, engaging stakeholders such as national health authorities, UN system organizations, bilateral development partners, academia, and civil society organizations. Interviews, testimonies, and quotations (with permission) are sought from these parties. The evaluation period is defined, and the WHO Representative (WR) in the country serves as the commissioner of the evaluation. The evaluation report should provide clear answers to the evaluation questions, supported by evidence, and include conclusions, lessons learned, and recommendations for the next CCS. It should contain an executive summary, methodology, findings, and recommendations. The report is submitted to senior management at the regional and headquarters levels. A debriefing session is organized at the end of the field visit to capture key points and discuss findings. The report is distributed to stakeholders and may be discussed at regional and global management forums. For internal learning purposes, a global webinar or seminar may be organized to share experiences and findings across the organization. The budget for the CCS review process should be included in the country biennial work plan or respective WHO regional budgets. Additional guidance is available in the WHO Evaluation Practice Handbook, which includes checklists, templates, and criteria for evaluation planning and reporting.
